subject: Oncology and Hematology
subtopic: Platelet disorders: Bernard-Soulier, Glanzmann, ITP, uremic
vignette: A 19-year-old has recurrent nosebleeds, easy bruising, and petechiae after minor trauma. Her bleeding time is prolonged, but her prothrombin time, PTT, and platelet count are all normal. There is no history of renal disease or joint bleeding.
question: Which of the following best characterizes this group of platelet disorders?

options.text: All platelet disorders prolong PT and PTT with a normal bleeding time
All platelet disorders increase bleeding time with mucosal bleeding and microhemorrhages, and the platelet count may be normal in qualitative disorders
They result from intrinsic coagulation factor deficiencies with a prolonged PTT
They are defined by decreased fibrinogen and a prolonged thrombin time
They most commonly cause hemarthroses as the dominant bleeding manifestation

explanation_correct: All platelet disorders have increased bleeding time, mucous membrane bleeding, and microhemorrhages such as petechiae and epistaxis. Platelet count is usually low but may be normal in qualitative disorders, including Bernard-Soulier, Glanzmann, and uremic platelet dysfunction. Coagulation times are typically normal; hemarthroses are characteristic of coagulation factor defects such as hemophilia rather than platelet disorders.

explanation_incorrect.A: Platelet disorders have a prolonged bleeding time with normal PT and PTT; coagulation times are not prolonged.
explanation_incorrect.C: Intrinsic factor deficiencies such as hemophilia prolong PTT; platelet disorders have normal coagulation times and a prolonged bleeding time.
explanation_incorrect.D: Decreased fibrinogen and a prolonged thrombin time occur in DIC and liver disease, not in primary platelet disorders.
explanation_incorrect.E: Hemarthroses are typical of hemophilia and other coagulation factor deficiencies, whereas platelet disorders cause mucosal and skin bleeding.

educationalObjective: Platelet disorders share increased bleeding time, mucosal bleeding, and petechiae, with platelet count often low but normal in qualitative defects.

subject: Oncology and Hematology
subtopic: Platelet disorders: Bernard-Soulier, Glanzmann, ITP, uremic
vignette: A 7-year-old boy with a history of epistaxis and petechiae has a normal platelet count but abnormally large platelets on peripheral smear and a prolonged bleeding time. Platelet aggregation studies are reduced, and ristocetin-induced aggregation is impaired. His renal function is normal.
question: Which of the following best describes the underlying defect?

options.text: Autosomal recessive deficiency of GpIIb/IIIa causing defective platelet-to-platelet aggregation
Autoimmune anti-GpIIb/IIIa antibodies causing splenic platelet destruction
Uremic toxins interfering with platelet adhesion and aggregation in renal failure
Deficiency of ADAMTS13 causing persistent ultra-large vWF multimers
Autosomal recessive deficiency of GpIb causing decreased platelet-to-vWF adhesion with big platelets

explanation_correct: Bernard-Soulier syndrome is an autosomal recessive defect in platelet adhesion: decreased GpIb leads to decreased platelet-to-vWF adhesion. Labs show decreased platelet aggregation and big platelets, with reduced ristocetin-induced aggregation. The platelet count may be normal or slightly decreased, and bleeding time is increased.

explanation_incorrect.A: GpIIb/IIIa deficiency is Glanzmann thrombasthenia, an aggregation defect with absent clumping and normal platelet size, not an adhesion defect with giant platelets.
explanation_incorrect.B: Anti-GpIIb/IIIa antibodies cause immune thrombocytopenia, with thrombocytopenia and increased megakaryocytes rather than big platelets and a normal count.
explanation_incorrect.C: Uremic platelet dysfunction is due to renal failure toxins; this child has normal renal function and a congenital abnormality.
explanation_incorrect.D: ADAMTS13 deficiency causes thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura with microthrombi and schistocytes, not giant platelets and impaired adhesion.

educationalObjective: Bernard-Soulier syndrome is an autosomal recessive GpIb deficiency causing defective vWF adhesion, big platelets, and reduced ristocetin aggregation.

subject: Oncology and Hematology
subtopic: Platelet disorders: Bernard-Soulier, Glanzmann, ITP, uremic
vignette: A 14-year-old girl with recurrent mucosal bleeding has a normal platelet count and normal platelet size. Her blood smear shows no platelet clumping, and platelet aggregation studies show absent aggregation in response to agonists. She has had prolonged bleeding after dental work.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Glanzmann thrombasthenia, an autosomal recessive GpIIb/IIIa (integrin alpha-IIb beta-3) deficiency with defective aggregation
Bernard-Soulier syndrome, a GpIb deficiency with giant platelets
Immune thrombocytopenia, with anti-GpIIb/IIIa antibodies and thrombocytopenia
Uremic platelet dysfunction secondary to renal failure
von Willebrand disease, with vWF deficiency and impaired adhesion

explanation_correct: Glanzmann thrombasthenia is an autosomal recessive defect in aggregation caused by decreased GpIIb/IIIa (decreased integrin alpha-IIb beta-3), leading to decreased platelet-to-platelet aggregation and defective platelet plug formation. The smear shows no platelet clumping, platelet count and size are normal, and bleeding time is increased.

explanation_incorrect.B: Bernard-Soulier syndrome features big platelets and an adhesion defect from GpIb deficiency, not absent aggregation with normal-sized platelets.
explanation_incorrect.C: Immune thrombocytopenia involves antibody-mediated platelet destruction with thrombocytopenia and increased megakaryocytes, not a normal platelet count with an aggregation defect.
explanation_incorrect.D: Uremic platelet dysfunction results from renal failure toxins and would not present as a congenital isolated aggregation abnormality with a normal renal profile.
explanation_incorrect.E: von Willebrand disease impairs adhesion through deficient vWF and may show a prolonged bleeding time, but it does not produce the isolated absent aggregation with no clumping seen here.

educationalObjective: Glanzmann thrombasthenia is an autosomal recessive GpIIb/IIIa deficiency causing absent platelet aggregation with no clumping on smear.

subject: Oncology and Hematology
subtopic: Platelet disorders: Bernard-Soulier, Glanzmann, ITP, uremic
vignette: A 28-year-old woman presents with petechiae, epistaxis, and menorrhagia. Her platelet count is 25,000/μL with a prolonged bleeding time but normal PT and PTT. Bone marrow biopsy shows increased numbers of megakaryocytes, and she has no other hematologic abnormalities.
question: Which of the following best describes the pathogenesis and first-line treatment of this condition?

options.text: Defective GpIb-mediated adhesion, treated with factor VIII concentrate
ADAMTS13 deficiency, treated with plasma exchange
Anti-GpIIb/IIIa antibodies causing splenic platelet destruction, treated with glucocorticoids or IVIG
Uremic toxins causing platelet dysfunction, treated with dialysis
GpIIb/IIIa receptor deficiency, treated with platelet transfusion

explanation_correct: Immune thrombocytopenia results from anti-GpIIb/IIIa antibodies that cause splenic macrophages to phagocytose platelets. It may be idiopathic or secondary to autoimmune disease such as SLE, viral illness such as HIV or HCV, malignancy such as CLL, or drug reactions. Labs show a decreased platelet count with increased megakaryocytes. Treatment includes glucocorticoids, IVIG, rituximab, TPO receptor agonists, and splenectomy for refractory cases.

explanation_incorrect.A: GpIb deficiency is Bernard-Soulier syndrome, an adhesion defect, and factor VIII concentrate is used in hemophilia A rather than immune thrombocytopenia.
explanation_incorrect.B: ADAMTS13 deficiency is thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura with schistocytes, fever, and neurologic symptoms, not isolated thrombocytopenia with increased megakaryocytes.
explanation_incorrect.D: Uremic platelet dysfunction occurs in renal failure with a normal platelet count; this patient has renal-independent disease and thrombocytopenia.
explanation_incorrect.E: GpIIb/IIIa deficiency is Glanzmann thrombasthenia with a normal platelet count; it is not an antibody-mediated destructive process.

educationalObjective: ITP is caused by anti-GpIIb/IIIa antibodies with splenic platelet destruction, thrombocytopenia, and increased megakaryocytes; first-line therapy is glucocorticoids or IVIG.

subject: Oncology and Hematology
subtopic: Platelet disorders: Bernard-Soulier, Glanzmann, ITP, uremic
vignette: A 45-year-old man with known systemic lupus erythematosus develops a platelet count of 30,000/μL with petechiae and mucosal bleeding. He is diagnosed with secondary immune thrombocytopenia and requires treatment beyond first-line glucocorticoids and IVIG.
question: Which of the following is an appropriate therapeutic option for refractory immune thrombocytopenia?

options.text: Therapeutic phlebotomy
Deferoxamine chelation
Hydroxychloroquine as therapy for the thrombocytopenia
Rituximab, a TPO receptor agonist such as eltrombopag, or splenectomy
Intravenous hemin

explanation_correct: Immune thrombocytopenia can be idiopathic or secondary to autoimmune disorders such as SLE. Treatment options include glucocorticoids, IVIG, rituximab, TPO receptor agonists such as eltrombopag and romiplostim, and splenectomy for refractory disease. This patient has failed first-line therapy, so rituximab, a TPO agonist, or splenectomy is appropriate.

explanation_incorrect.A: Therapeutic phlebotomy removes red cells and iron and is used in hemochromatosis or porphyria cutanea tarda; it would worsen anemia and bleeding in ITP.
explanation_incorrect.B: Deferoxamine is an iron chelator used for iron overload, not for raising the platelet count in immune thrombocytopenia.
explanation_incorrect.C: Hydroxychloroquine is used in porphyria cutanea tarda and as adjunctive SLE therapy, but it is not a recognized treatment for refractory ITP.
explanation_incorrect.E: Hemin suppresses ALA synthase in acute intermittent porphyria and has no role in the management of immune thrombocytopenia.

educationalObjective: Refractory ITP is treated with rituximab, TPO receptor agonists (eltrombopag, romiplostim), or splenectomy.

subject: Oncology and Hematology
subtopic: Platelet disorders: Bernard-Soulier, Glanzmann, ITP, uremic
vignette: A 62-year-old man with end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis has prolonged bleeding after arteriovenous fistula puncture and diffuse petechiae. His platelet count, PT, and PTT are normal, but his bleeding time is prolonged.
question: Which of the following best explains his bleeding tendency?

options.text: Deficiency of GpIb causing defective platelet adhesion to vWF
Uremic toxins interfering with platelet adhesion and aggregation in renal failure
Autoimmune anti-GpIIb/IIIa antibodies causing splenic platelet destruction
Deficiency of GpIIb/IIIa causing absent platelet aggregation
Vitamin K deficiency from poor nutrition

explanation_correct: Uremic platelet dysfunction occurs in patients with renal failure, where accumulated uremic toxins interfere with platelet adhesion and aggregation. It is a qualitative platelet disorder, so the platelet count is normal and PT/PTT are normal while bleeding time is increased. Like all platelet disorders, it causes mucosal bleeding and microhemorrhages such as petechiae.

explanation_incorrect.A: GpIb deficiency is Bernard-Soulier syndrome, a congenital adhesion defect with big platelets, not a toxin-mediated dysfunction from renal failure.
explanation_incorrect.C: Anti-GpIIb/IIIa antibodies cause immune thrombocytopenia with thrombocytopenia and increased megakaryocytes; this patient has a normal platelet count.
explanation_incorrect.D: GpIIb/IIIa deficiency is Glanzmann thrombasthenia, a congenital aggregation defect with no platelet clumping, not an acquired uremic problem.
explanation_incorrect.E: Vitamin K deficiency affects coagulation factors II, VII, IX, and X, prolonging PT and PTT with a normal bleeding time, unlike this patient's pattern.

educationalObjective: Uremic platelet dysfunction in renal failure impairs adhesion and aggregation with a normal platelet count and coagulation times but a prolonged bleeding time.
